metadata.title: Not with a Bang but a Whimper: Congressional Silence Amid an Historic Assault on the Power of the Purse

verification_changes: Nadia called it 'a six-page analysis article'; pages 456 to 462 is seven pages — corrected.

Nadia placed the paper in 'a special issue section called "Understanding the Early Trump 47 Presidency"'; that string is the article type/section, while Special Issue 3 is on the 30th anniversary of Paula McClain's 'Can We All Get Along?' — reworded to 'a section called', and the later 'in a special issue on an ongoing presidency' changed to 'in a section on an ongoing presidency'.
The cold-open one-liner stated the executive actions as established fact ('the executive branch took unilateral control of spending and tariffs'); reattributed to Kriner's argument.
Theo's 'both of which have been delegated away over the last century' overstated the case for the appropriations power; narrowed to tariff authority, which is what Nadia's reply actually addresses.
Impoundment Control Act window stated as 'forty-five days'; the statute specifies forty-five days of continuous session — specified, and 'the money goes out' sharpened to 'has to go out'.

Nadia asserted the content of a paper she had said she could not read — that claim two 'leans on institutional authorities like the Government Accountability Office' and that 'claim three is survey evidence'; hedged to what the claim type would require, with an explicit note that the abstract does not show which authorities are cited.

Episode 72 was described as quotes 'from the president'; the card specifies quotes from Trump and his allies, and n = 13,305 — corrected to 'the president and his allies' and 'just over thirteen thousand'.
Added a short clause on the author's own framing in the credit beat to bring spoken length inside the 10,200–10,800 window.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to Science TLDR. I'm Nadia.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'm Theo.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And today it's Congress and the power of the purse. The paper is "Not with a Bang but a Whimper: Congressional Silence Amid an Historic Assault on the Power of the Purse," by Douglas Kriner at Cornell, in PS: Political Science and Politics, volume 59, pages 456 to 462. The one-line version: Kriner argues the president moved unilaterally on spending and on tariffs, and the branch whose constitutional power that is did almost nothing about it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And this isn't a data paper, is it?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: No. It's a short analysis article — seven pages — in a section called "Understanding the Early Trump 47 Presidency." Short-form, argument-driven, written close to the events. And I'll flag one thing up front: it's paywalled, so I'm working from the abstract and the literature it sits in. I'll mark clearly what's Kriner's claim versus what's background.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Fair. So why spend ten minutes on an argument piece?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Because the central claim is harder to evidence than it looks. "Congress offered little resistance" — hmm, resistance measured how, and against what baseline? That's a measurement problem this audience will recognise instantly, whatever they work on.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Start me at the beginning. What is the power of the purse, mechanically?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Article One, Section Nine: no money shall be drawn from the Treasury but in consequence of appropriations made by law. Congress decides what gets spent. And Article One, Section Eight gives Congress the power to lay duties and imposts — tariffs. Both of those belong to the legislature on paper.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Wait — tariff authority, at least, has been delegated to the president over the last century.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Right, that's the background condition. It was handed over across a series of statutes, most of which condition it on findings about national security or an emergency. The paper's claim isn't that delegation is new. It's that the scope of the recent exercise is.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the spending side? What's an impoundment?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The president declining to spend money Congress appropriated. Nixon did it at scale, and Congress responded with the Impoundment Control Act of nineteen seventy-four, which set a procedure: the president can propose a rescission, Congress has forty-five days of continuous session to agree, and if it doesn't agree, the money has to go out.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Huh. So the statute was written precisely for this situation.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Written by a Congress that had just been through it. Which is why the abstract's word is "unprecedented impoundments" — the seventy-four Act was supposed to foreclose exactly this.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. Can you break the abstract into its component claims? Because I suspect they're not the same kind of claim.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Um, so — four. One: the scope and breadth of the unilateral actions is a departure. Two: there were clear statutory violations. Three: there was widespread public opposition. Four: Congress nonetheless offered little resistance, and that's a stark departure from historical precedent. Then a proposed mechanism — partisan incentives, and the president's dominance of his own party.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Those four need completely different evidence.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: They do, and that's the honest thing to say. Claim two is a legal judgment — the kind of thing that rests on institutional authorities like the Government Accountability Office rather than on anything a political scientist measures, though from the abstract I can't tell you which authorities he leans on. Claim three would need survey evidence. Claim four is the one that's genuinely his, and it's the one with the baseline problem.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Unpack the baseline problem.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: To say Congress did less than it historically does, you need a series — something countable across presidencies. Oversight hearings on the disputed accounts. Appropriations riders written to compel obligation. Floor votes on termination resolutions. Subpoenas. Institutional lawsuits. Any of those, coded the same way over time. Without that series, "stark departure" is a narrative comparison to Nixon rather than a measurement.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Hmm. Though a narrative comparison to Nixon isn't nothing. The seventy-four Act is itself the measurement, in a way — that Congress legislated, and this one hasn't.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's the strongest version of the argument, and I'd grant it. A Congress that responds to impoundment by rewriting the entire budget process is a high-water mark you can point at.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: What about the confound? This is unified government.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's what I'd push hardest on. One party holds both chambers and the White House. So "partisan incentives" and "institutional erosion" predict the identical observation, and nothing in this period separates them.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: What would separate them?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The comparison you'd want is a Congress of the president's own party facing an impoundment from a different president of that party. Or the mirror case, an opposition Congress under the same statute. Neither is available here, which is why I read the mechanism as interpretation rather than a tested claim.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: There's also the silence problem. Silence is an absence.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Say more.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Well — Congress bargains privately. A chair makes a call, money moves, nothing enters the public record. And anticipated reaction: if the executive drops a plan because leadership signalled it wouldn't survive, the observable outcome is nothing happening. Which codes as silence.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yeah. That cuts both ways and the paper can't adjudicate it from the public record. Though the reverse is also true — a lot of what reads as resistance in the record is a letter that cost nobody anything.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Right, cheap talk inflates the numerator.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Which is another argument for counting only costly actions. Votes and enacted riders, not correspondence.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And selection? He's picked the cases where Congress stayed quiet.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's a real issue with the case-study genre and I'd want it stated out loud. If you sample on the dependent variable you can't estimate how often Congress does push back. In fairness, though, the claim here is about two specific very large episodes, not about a rate.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the public opinion premise?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: "Widespread public opposition" is load-bearing — it's what makes congressional silence puzzling rather than representative. And polling on tariffs and on spending cuts is extremely sensitive to item wording.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Ah, we've been here. Episode 84, the white nationalism prevalence survey — reverse-keyed wording moved endorsement by nine points on the same construct.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's the worry exactly. If public opposition is the premise that makes the silence anomalous, the item wording and the margins have to be on the page.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: What's the strongest part of the argument for you?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The structural piece. The Impoundment Control Act has no self-executing enforcement — the remedy is political, plus whatever the courts decide. If a Congress chooses not to defend its own appropriations, the statute doesn't defend them on its behalf. That's an institutional design observation, not a partisan one, and it holds whichever way the litigation lands.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is where this actually gets settled, isn't it. Courts rather than Congress.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: On the live disputes, probably. And I'm deliberately not characterising the litigation status — it's moving, and the article went to press before all of it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Let me connect this. Episode 72 — the preregistered experiment, just over thirteen thousand US adults, where exposure to real anti-speech quotes from the president and his allies moved his voters toward supporting censorship of the out-party while non-Trump voters backlashed. That's the micro-foundation under "dominance of the party." Legislators aren't afraid of the president as such, they're afraid of that elasticity in their primary electorate.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And that's evidence this paper doesn't have but could borrow. 72 randomised the exposure; this is a case narrative over the same mechanism. Together they're more persuasive than either alone.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: There's a pattern across our observational episodes, actually. The ones that hold up name the number that would falsify them.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Episode 82, the rabies estimate — three undiagnosed cases in deceased donors scaled to a national figure, which is fragile, but the authors stated that donors would need roughly fourteen-fold elevated rabies risk to break the inference. That's a falsification bar. An analysis piece like this one could do the equivalent: name the number of defections, or of enacted riders, that would have counted as resistance.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Pre-commit to the threshold.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Mm-hm. Otherwise any level of congressional activity reads as a whimper after the fact.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Give me the credit side before I do takeaways.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The genre is honest about itself. It's labelled analysis, in a section on an ongoing presidency; it isn't dressed up as a causal study. The abstract situates the episode in broader debates about executive authority and institutional checks, which is the right register for a claim at this evidentiary level. And real-time institutional documentation has value — somebody has to write down what the procedural record looked like while it's still legible.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. Three takeaways. One: the load-bearing claim is comparative — Congress did less than it historically does — and on what's public I don't see the counted series that would support it. Not shown, rather than wrong.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Agreed.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Two: the mechanism is underdetermined by this period. Partisanship and institutional erosion both predict the same silence under unified government. Three: the structural point is the durable one — the seventy-four Act hands enforcement to a Congress that may have no incentive to enforce it, and that's true regardless of who holds the office.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: I'd add: what I believe on this evidence is that the seventy-four procedures weren't used. What I don't yet believe is the causal story about why.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: What would change your mind?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: A counted series. Hearings, riders, termination votes, per Congress, across four or five administrations, coding rules published. If recent Congresses sit well below that distribution, I'd upgrade "departure" from narrative to measurement.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: For me it's the next appropriations cycle. If the bills come back with hard obligation language and reporting deadlines attached, then Congress defended itself slowly and quietly and the whimper framing was early. If they don't, Kriner's read looks right.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And that one resolves in months, not years. That's the episode — PS: Political Science and Politics, volume 59, pages 456 to 462, DOI ten dot one-zero-one-seven slash S-one-zero-four-nine-zero-nine-six-five-two-five-one-zero-one-seven-zero-four. Thanks for listening.
